name: LGD-2941

lead: LGD-2941 (also LGD-122941) is a nonsteroidal SARM of the quinolinone class, explored for muscle wasting, low testosterone and bone loss. Muscle-building communities treat it as a lean mass candidate.

Like other SARMs, it is designed to activate the androgen receptor selectively in muscle and bone, the chain being anabolic signalling in muscle and more lean mass. Its development has reportedly stopped after a Phase I trial was discontinued. Very little is published beyond its chemistry, and no human results were identified.

paras: There is little community material and no established routine for appearance use.
No safety data are public. It is unapproved, and SARMs generally are banned in sport.

angle.text: LGD-2941 is a quinolinone SARM that muscle-building communities treat as a lean mass candidate, designed to activate the androgen receptor selectively in muscle. It was investigated for cachexia and hypogonadism, then discontinued after Phase I.

lead: LGD-2941 (also LGD-122941) is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the quinolinone class that was studied for cachexia, sexual dysfunction, hypogonadism, menopause and osteoporosis.[1][2] SARMs are designed to activate the androgen receptor in muscle and bone while having less effect on the prostate, which is the reason bodybuilders and athletes take an interest in the class for muscle and leanness.[2]

Wikipedia reports that LGD-2941 is no longer being developed, and its Phase I trial was discontinued.[1][2] Little published information exists beyond its chemistry; a 2008 Bioorganic and Medicinal Chemistry Letters paper on related oxazinoquinolinone SARMs is the main cited literature.[1] No community material or human results were identified for this specific compound.
infobox: Discontinued after Phase I; never approved

paras: As a SARM, it is designed to act as an agonist at the androgen receptor in bone and muscle and as a partial agonist or antagonist in tissues such as the prostate. One proposed reason for the selectivity is that 5-alpha reductase does not activate SARMs the way it converts testosterone to DHT; the mechanism is described as still debated.[2]
It is a quinolinone derivative bearing a pyrrolidine ring and trifluoromethyl groups, with a molar mass of about 394 g/mol.[1]

The first nonsteroidal SARMs appeared in 1998 from the University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals, and the term was introduced in 1999; David Handelsman has called it a misleading pharmaceutical marketing term.[2] Wikipedia lists LGD-2941 as discontinued after Phase I, and describes LGD-4033 (ligandrol) as reaching Phase II.[2]

As of 2023 neither the FDA nor the EMA had approved any SARM. The World Anti-Doping Agency banned SARMs in 2008, and in the class, trials reported raised liver enzymes, lowered HDL cholesterol and suppression of testosterone, with case reports linking recreational use to liver injury.[2]

No studies found. A Phase I trial is reported to have been discontinued, and no results were identified.[2] Early trials of other SARMs (enobosarm and others) reported increased lean body mass and muscle size.[2]

timeline.event: First nonsteroidal SARMs appear from the University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals.[2]
A paper on related oxazinoquinolinone SARMs is published; WADA bans SARMs.[1][2]
